blocks.text:
A test suite has two jobs: it detects regressions quickly, and it documents intended behaviour in executable form. A suite that is slow, flaky or coupled to implementation details fails both jobs, because developers stop running it or stop trusting it. Test design therefore starts with a strategy: which behaviour is verified at which level, at what cost, and with which tools. This chapter fixes the strategy and then treats the lowest level in depth: unit tests written with JUnit 5, AssertJ and Mockito, including the handling of time, randomness and test data. The Spring-specific levels are covered in the chapters that follow.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The test pyramid and its cost model

Tests differ along three axes: scope (how much real code runs), speed (milliseconds against seconds or minutes) and diagnostic precision (a failing unit test names a method; a failing end-to-end test names a symptom). The test pyramid allocates many cheap, precise tests at the base and few expensive, broad tests at the top. For a Spring Boot service, the levels map onto tools as follows.

blocks.text:
The pyramid is a heuristic rather than a law. Services that consist mostly of data access and little logic gain more from integration tests against a real database than from mocked unit tests; the shape is then closer to a "honeycomb" with a thick middle layer. The governing rule is to test each behaviour at the lowest level that can exhibit the failure. A pricing rule is a unit-level concern. A mapping that depends on PostgreSQL column types is not, because no mock reproduces that behaviour.

#### JUnit 5 architecture

JUnit 5 consists of three components. The **JUnit Platform** is the launcher and the `TestEngine` SPI used by build tools and IDEs. **JUnit Jupiter** is the programming model (`@Test`, extensions) together with its engine. **JUnit Vintage** runs JUnit 3 and 4 tests on the same platform. Spring Boot's `spring-boot-starter-test` brings Jupiter, AssertJ, Mockito, Hamcrest, JSONassert, JsonPath and the Spring test support.

The central lifecycle rule is that Jupiter creates a **new instance of the test class for every test method** (`@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_METHOD)`, the default). Instance fields therefore cannot leak state between tests, and `@BeforeEach` runs against a fresh object. `@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll` run once per class and must be `static` unless the class is annotated `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`. The following program reproduces this mechanism in about forty lines of plain JDK code: it finds annotated methods by reflection, creates a new instance per test and runs the callbacks around the test body.

blocks.title: MiniJUnit.java

$ java MiniJUnit.java
startsAtZero
  setUp
  PASS
  tearDown
incrementsOnce
  setUp
  PASS
  tearDown
deliberatelyFailing
  setUp
  FAIL: expected 2
  tearDown
2 passed, 1 failed
blocks.title: Output of the harness (real run; method order from reflection is not specified and may differ)

blocks.text: The harness omits what the real engine adds: extension points (`BeforeEachCallback`, `ParameterResolver`, `TestExecutionExceptionHandler`), parameter injection, nested classes, conditional execution, parallelism and reporting. Spring's `SpringExtension` is an ordinary Jupiter extension; it builds or fetches the `ApplicationContext` in `postProcessTestInstance` and injects fields and parameters from it. Order of test methods in Jupiter is deterministic but intentionally non-obvious; tests must not depend on it, and `@TestMethodOrder` exists for the rare exception.

blocks.text:
#### Writing readable tests with Jupiter and AssertJ

Jupiter supplies several constructs that reduce duplication without hiding intent.

- `@ParameterizedTest` runs one method against many inputs. Sources: `@ValueSource`, `@CsvSource`, `@MethodSource`, `@EnumSource`.
- `@Nested` classes group the cases of one scenario (for example "when the cart is empty") and inherit the enclosing `@BeforeEach`.
- `@DisplayName` and `@Tag` control reporting and selection (for example `-Dgroups=slow` with Surefire).
- `@TempDir` supplies an isolated directory; `@Timeout` fails a test that runs too long.
- `assertThrows` and `assertAll` in Jupiter, or the richer AssertJ equivalents.

AssertJ is preferred for assertions because the fluent API is discoverable in the IDE and failure messages show actual and expected values. The pattern `assertThat(actual).isEqualTo(expected)` is the entry point; `extracting`, `containsExactly`, `usingRecursiveComparison` and `assertThatThrownBy` cover most needs. Two details cause frequent confusion. First, `BigDecimal.equals` compares scale: `new BigDecimal("180.0000")` is not equal to `new` `BigDecimal("180.00")`; the AssertJ method `isEqualByComparingTo` compares numeric value. Second, `SoftAssertions` collect every failure of a block instead of stopping at the first, which shortens the edit-run cycle when several fields of a result are verified.

#### Test doubles with Mockito

A **test double** replaces a collaborator. The vocabulary (after Meszaros) distinguishes a dummy (passed but unused), a stub (returns canned answers), a spy (wraps a real object and records calls), a mock (verifies interactions) and a fake (a working lightweight implementation such as an in-memory repository). Mockito creates stubs, spies and mocks.

Mockito 5 uses the inline mock maker by default, which instruments classes through a Java agent and therefore mocks final classes, final methods and (with `mockStatic`) static methods. The generated mock records every invocation, matches stubbing rules in the order they were declared (the last matching rule wins), and returns type-appropriate defaults (`null`, `0`, `false`, empty collection, empty `Optional`) for unstubbed calls. The plain-JDK program below implements the same idea with `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`: an `InvocationHandler` records calls and arguments and returns a configured answer. It also shows the standard technique for time: a `java.time.Clock` is injected, and tests supply `Clock.fixed`.

blocks.title: MiniMock.java

blocks.code:
$ java MiniMock.java
calls     = [charge, charge]
captured  = 180.0000 , 200.00
verify times(2) -> true
blocks.title: Output (real run)

blocks.text: The captured amounts show the `BigDecimal` scale effect described above: multiplying `200.00` by `0.90` yields scale 4. A test asserting `isEqualTo(new BigDecimal("180.00"))` fails, while `isEqualByComparingTo("180.00")` passes. The program also demonstrates why `Clock` injection makes the promotion boundary testable without sleeping or touching the system clock.

blocks.text:
#### Mockito rules that prevent fragile tests

- Use `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`. It installs **strict stubs**: an unused stubbing raises `UnnecessaryStubbingException`, and a stubbed call made with different arguments raises `PotentialStubbingProblem`. Both indicate dead or wrong test setup.
- Mock only collaborators that cross a boundary (repository, HTTP client, clock, message sender). Do not mock value objects, records, collections or the class under test.
- Verify outcomes before interactions. `verify(gateway).charge(...)` is appropriate for a side effect that is the observable result (a payment was requested). Verifying every internal call couples the test to the implementation and breaks on refactoring.
- Use `ArgumentCaptor` when the argument is constructed inside the unit and its content matters.
- Prefer `doReturn(x).when(spy).method()` for spies, because `when(spy.method())` executes the real method during stubbing.
- Never share a mock between tests through a static field.

#### Time, randomness and test data

Non-deterministic inputs are the second most common cause of flaky tests, after shared state. The remedy is the same for all of them: pass the source of non-determinism in as a dependency. Time is injected as `java.time.Clock` (a `@Bean` in production, `Clock.fixed` or `Clock.offset` in tests). Randomness is injected as a `java.util.random.RandomGenerator` or a seeded `java.util.Random`. Identifiers are injected as a `Supplier<UUID>`. Scheduling is tested by invoking the scheduled method directly rather than waiting for the trigger.

**Test data builders** keep fixtures readable. A builder supplies valid defaults and lets each test override only the fields relevant to the scenario, so the intent of the test is visible and a new mandatory field is added in one place.

blocks.text:
Mutation testing complements coverage. Line coverage reports which code ran, not whether any assertion would notice a defect. PIT (`pitest-maven`) mutates the bytecode (flips a comparison, removes a call, changes a constant) and re-runs the tests; a mutant that no test kills indicates a missing assertion. The cost is a long run, so PIT is normally applied to the domain package or to changed files in continuous integration.

### Worked example

The service under test calculates an order total with a coupon and charges a gateway. The listing shows the production class and its JUnit 5, AssertJ and Mockito test. The code is idiomatic for Spring Boot 3.x on JDK 21; it was not executed on the build machine, because the Spring and Mockito artefacts are not available offline (the mechanisms above were executed with plain-JDK equivalents).

PricingServiceTest.java

What to notice: the clock is fixed at one instant, so the expiry boundary (one second before and after) is tested exactly; `isEqualByComparingTo` avoids the scale pitfall; the parameterized test covers three rounding cases with one method; strict stubs fail the build if a stubbing becomes unused after a refactoring.

### Hands-on

Unit tests are executed by the Maven Surefire plugin (`mvn test`) or the Gradle `test` task. Integration tests conventionally use the suffix `IT` and run in the Failsafe plugin (`mvn verify`), which keeps the fast loop fast.

blocks.title: junit-platform.properties

blocks.text:
With these settings, test classes run concurrently while the methods of one class run sequentially. Parallelism is safe only when tests share no mutable state; the next section shows what happens otherwise.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: A test suite fails intermittently after parallel execution is enabled

**Scenario.** A team enables class-level parallelism to shorten a six-minute build. The suite passes locally and fails on roughly one pipeline run in a hundred, with different tests failing each time.

**Symptoms.** Assertion failures such as `expected size 1 but was 2` that do not reproduce when a single test is re-run. The failures disappear with `junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled=false`.

**Diagnosis.** (1) Re-run the failing class alone ten times; if it is stable, the cause lies in interaction with other tests. (2) Search the test and main sources for `static` mutable fields, singletons and caches: `grep -rn` `"static.*\(List\|Map\|Set\)<" src`. (3) Run with `-Djunit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.classes.default=same_thread` to confirm. (4) Order the suspects by reading `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` blocks that clear shared structures.

The following program reproduces the mechanism: two tests clear and fill the same static list. Executed one after another they always pass; executed on two threads the interleaving corrupts the list.

blocks.title: FlakyDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ for i in 1 2 3; do java FlakyDemo.java | grep parallel; done
parallel  : 0 failing suites out of 200
parallel  : 1 failing suites out of 200
parallel  : 0 failing suites out of 200
blocks.title: Three consecutive runs (real; the parallel figure varies between runs, which is the defect)

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** Shared mutable state with no synchronisation. The failure probability per run is small, which is why it survives code review and local runs, and why it is expensive to find by retrying.

**Fix.** Remove the shared state: create collaborators per test (fields of the test instance are per-test under the default lifecycle), replace static caches with injected beans, and use `@ResourceLock("shared-resource")` from Jupiter for the rare unavoidable shared resource such as a port or a system property. Do not add retries to hide the failure.

**Prevention.** Enable parallel execution early, while the suite is small. Treat any test that needs a specific execution order as defective. Keep a CI report of per-test failure rates (Surefire XML reports) so that a test failing in 1 of 200 runs is visible.

blocks.text:
#### Problem 2: A time-dependent test fails every day after midnight UTC

**Scenario.** A test creates an order and asserts that `order.createdAt().toLocalDate()` equals `LocalDate.now()`. It fails in the nightly build, which starts at 00:00:03 UTC on a server in another time zone.

**Symptoms.** The failure occurs only within a window of a few seconds or hours each day, and only on some machines.

**Diagnosis.** Search for `LocalDate.now()`, `Instant.now()`, `System.currentTimeMillis()` and `new Date()` in both main and test code. Check the JVM default time zone (`-Duser.timezone`, the `TZ` variable) on the failing agent. Compare the timestamps in the assertion message.

**Root cause.** The production code and the test each read the system clock independently, and a day boundary falls between the two reads; in addition, the two reads may use different zones.

**Fix.** Inject one `Clock` into the production code, read the time once, and construct the test with `Clock.fixed`.

blocks.title: ClockConfig.java

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Forbid direct calls to the static `now()` methods outside the configuration class by an ArchUnit rule or a Checkstyle regular expression. Tests that need a Spring context replace the `Clock` bean with a `@TestConfiguration` that returns a fixed clock.

#### Problem 3: A mock-heavy test passes while the production code is broken

**Scenario.** After a refactoring that renamed a repository method, all unit tests of the service remain green but the endpoint returns HTTP 500 in the staging environment.

**Symptoms.** High line coverage, no failing test, and a failing deployed application. The stack trace points at a query that Spring Data cannot derive (`PropertyReferenceException`).

**Diagnosis.** The test stubs `repository.findByEmailAddress(...)`, a method on a mocked interface. A mock accepts any method signature declared on the interface, so it cannot detect that Spring Data derives the query from the method name and the entity has no `emailAddress` property.

**Root cause.** The test verified the interaction with a double that cannot reproduce the behaviour that failed. The behaviour belongs to the persistence layer and must be tested there.

**Fix.** Keep the service unit test, and add a slice or integration test (`@DataJpaTest` with a real database; see the chapters that follow) that executes each repository method. A single context start-up detects invalid derived queries, because Spring Data validates them when the repository bean is created.

**Prevention.** Apply the rule from the pyramid section: assert each behaviour at the lowest level that can fail for that reason. Mock the repository in service tests, but test the repository against a real database.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between a mock, a stub and a spy?

A stub returns canned answers and is not asserted upon. A mock is a double whose interactions are verified. A spy wraps a real object, so unstubbed calls execute real code while calls are still recorded. Mockito uses the term "mock" for objects that act as stubs or mocks depending on whether the test calls `verify`.

#### Why does JUnit 5 create a new instance of the test class for each test method?

Isolation: instance fields cannot carry state from one test to another, and the order of execution does not matter. `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` changes this behaviour and makes `@BeforeAll` non-static, but also makes shared state the responsibility of the test author.

#### What does MockitoExtension add compared with MockitoAnnotations.openMocks?

It integrates with the Jupiter lifecycle, closes the mocks after each test and applies strict stubs by default, so unused or mismatched stubbings fail the test.

#### How is code that depends on the current time tested?

By injecting a `java.time.Clock` and substituting `Clock.fixed` or `Clock.offset` in tests. Sleeping, comparing against the real clock with tolerances, and mocking static methods are inferior alternatives.

#### Which tests belong at the base of the pyramid, and why not test everything end to end?

Business rules, mappers, validators and algorithms belong at the base because they run in milliseconds and fail with a precise location. End-to-end tests are slow, depend on every component and fail for environmental reasons; they verify a few critical journeys only.

#### Does 100 percent line coverage prove the tests are adequate?

No. Coverage measures executed lines, not asserted behaviour. A test without assertions can reach full coverage. Mutation testing (PIT) estimates assertion quality by checking whether the tests detect injected defects.

#### How are void methods and exceptions verified?

Void methods through their side effects (`verify`, captured arguments, state of a fake) and exceptions with `assertThrows` or `assertThatThrownBy`, which also permit assertions on type, message and cause.

#### When should a spy be used?

Rarely: for legacy classes that cannot be split, or to verify a call on a real object while keeping its behaviour. Frequent need for spies on the class under test indicates a design problem (the class does too much).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Test each behaviour at the lowest level that can fail for that reason; use the pyramid as a budget for cost and speed, not as a fixed ratio.
- Jupiter creates one test instance per method; shared mutable state, static caches and ordering assumptions are the main sources of flaky tests.
- Inject `Clock`, random generators and identifier suppliers; then time and randomness become ordinary inputs.
- Use `MockitoExtension` with strict stubs; mock boundaries, not value objects, and avoid verifying internals.
- Compare `BigDecimal` values with `isEqualByComparingTo`; `equals` includes scale.
- Mocks cannot detect persistence or serialisation defects; those need slice or integration tests.

sections.title: Spring Slice Tests and Context Caching

blocks.text:
Unit tests prove that a class behaves correctly in isolation; they cannot prove that the annotations around it work. Request mapping, JSON binding, validation, exception translation, derived queries and transaction boundaries are all declared in annotations and executed by framework code, so a test must run some of the Spring infrastructure to verify them. Starting the full application for every such test is wasteful. Spring Boot therefore provides **test slices**: annotations that start a deliberately small application context containing one layer (web, persistence, JSON, HTTP client) and nothing else. This chapter explains how slices are built, what each one contains, how the test context cache decides whether to reuse a context, and why suites become slow when it does not.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Anatomy of a Spring Boot test

A test class annotated with a Boot test annotation is processed by the Spring TestContext Framework. The sequence is as follows.

1. `SpringExtension` (the Jupiter extension, registered by the meta-annotation `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)` on every Boot test annotation) asks the `TestContextManager` for a `TestContext`.
2. The `TestContextManager` builds a `MergedContextConfiguration` from the annotations on the class: configuration classes, active profiles, property sources, `ContextCustomizer` instances (contributed by `@MockitoBean`, `@DynamicPropertySource`, the Testcontainers support and others) and the `ContextLoader`. For Boot tests the loader is `SpringBootContextLoader`.
3. The `DefaultCacheAwareContextLoaderDelegate` looks up this configuration in the **context cache** (`DefaultContextCache`). A hit returns the existing `ApplicationContext`; a miss loads a new one through `SpringApplication` and stores it.
4. `DependencyInjectionTestExecutionListener` injects `@Autowired` fields and parameters of the test instance from the context. Other listeners handle transactions (`TransactionalTestExecutionListener`), `@Sql` scripts and dirty-context handling.

The cache key is the `MergedContextConfiguration`. Two test classes share a context only when every component of the key is equal. The practical consequence is that a different set of `@MockitoBean` declarations, a different `@TestPropertySource`, a different profile list or a different `@Import` produces a new context with a full start-up. The cache holds 32 contexts by default and evicts the least recently used (`spring.test.context.cache.maxSize`).

blocks.text: The next program models the cache faithfully enough to show the cost structure. The key is a record of configuration class, mock set and properties; a miss costs 150 ms (standing for a context start), a hit costs nothing.

blocks.title: ContextCacheDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java ContextCacheDemo.java
test classes     : 7
context start-ups: 4 (distinct keys: 4)
elapsed          : ~600 ms
shared config    : 1 start-up, ~150 ms
blocks.title: Output (real run; the elapsed figures are rounded)

blocks.text:
Seven test classes cost four start-ups because four distinct keys exist. In a real application a start-up takes two to fifteen seconds rather than 150 ms, so the arithmetic dominates the build time. The remedy is structural: keep the number of distinct configurations small.

#### What each slice loads

A slice annotation combines three things: a `@TypeExcludeFilter` that restricts component scanning to the relevant stereotypes, an `@AutoConfigure...` set that enables only the relevant auto-configuration classes (listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure...imports` files), and default properties. Anything outside the slice is absent from the context and must be supplied by `@MockitoBean`, `@Import` or `@TestConfiguration`.

rows: `@Controller`, `@ControllerAdvice`, `@JsonComponent`, `Converter`, `Filter`, `HandlerInterceptor`, `WebMvcConfigurer`; MVC, Jackson, validation, MockMvc, Spring Security
`@Entity` scan, Spring Data repositories, DataSource, Hibernate, `TestEntityManager`, Flyway or Liquibase
blocks.caption: Slice annotations (Boot 3.4 and 3.5).

blocks.text:
In Boot 3.x these annotations live in `org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure...` packages (for example `org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest`). Spring Boot 4 reorganised the test modules and moved several of them (for example the web slice moved to a `webmvc.test.autoconfigure` package); code in this chapter targets Boot 3.4 and 3.5.

A slice never contains the services that a controller calls. A controller test that omits `@MockitoBean` for its service fails at context start with `UnsatisfiedDependencyException` naming the missing bean. This is a feature: the failure message lists exactly the collaborators the layer needs.

#### @MockitoBean, @MockitoSpyBean and @MockBean

Spring Framework 6.2 introduced bean override support: `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean` in the package `org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito`. Boot 3.4 deprecated the older `@MockBean` and `@SpyBean` (package `org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito`), whose behaviour the new annotations replace; removal is announced for Boot 4. Differences that matter: `@MockitoBean` can be declared on the test class as well as on fields, replaces or creates the bean by type or name, and registers its definition through a `ContextCustomizer`, so the declared set is part of the cache key. Mocks are reset after each test by default (`MockReset.AFTER`).

#### MockMvc, MockMvcTester and the real server

`MockMvc` drives the `DispatcherServlet` directly through a mock servlet request and response. No socket is opened and no Tomcat runs; filters, interceptors, argument resolution, message conversion and exception handlers all execute, because they belong to the Spring MVC pipeline. What is **not** exercised: the servlet container (error pages, `server.*` properties, HTTP/2, compression), real serialisation over the wire and multi-threaded behaviour. `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with `TestRestTemplate` or `RestClient` covers those.

blocks.text:
`MockMvcTester` (Spring Framework 6.2, therefore Boot 3.4 and later) is an AssertJ-based facade over `MockMvc`. It replaces the `andExpect(...)` chain with `assertThat(...)`, gives better failure messages and treats exceptions raised by the handler as assertion targets (`hasFailed()`, `failure()`). It is auto-configured by `@WebMvcTest` when AssertJ is on the classpath.

### Worked example

The scenario is an order endpoint: `POST /orders` validates the body, delegates to `OrderService` and returns `201` with the created resource, while `GET /orders/{id}` returns `404` as an RFC 9457 `ProblemDetail` for an unknown identifier. The production code is shown first.

What to notice: no `@SpringBootTest`, hence no database and no unrelated beans; the `400` test needs no stubbing because validation fails before the service is called; the `404` test verifies the advice and the `ProblemDetail` serialisation together. Content type `application/problem+json` is also asserted in a complete suite (`hasContentType`).

#### Persistence slice with a real database

`@DataJpaTest` configures an in-memory database by default (`@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = ANY)`), wraps each test in a transaction that is rolled back, and exposes `TestEntityManager`. The default replacement is a hazard when production uses PostgreSQL, as discussed in the problems below. With Testcontainers the replacement is switched off so that the container database is used.

blocks.title: OrderRepositoryTest.java

blocks.text:
The calls `em.flush()` and `em.clear()` are essential: without them the persistence context returns the managed instance from the first-level cache and the test never reads the database, so a wrong query or a mapping error remains undetected.

Two further slices are small and fast. `@JsonTest` verifies serialisation contracts (field names, date formats, `@JsonIgnore`) through `JacksonTester<T>` without any web layer. `@RestClientTest(PaymentClient.class)` binds a `MockRestServiceServer` to the client's `RestClient.Builder` so that URL, headers and response mapping of an outgoing call are verified with canned responses.

### Hands-on

Running a single slice test and inspecting the context start-up is the quickest way to learn what a slice contains. The condition evaluation report lists the auto-configurations that matched; for a web slice, no `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` entry appears under "Positive matches".

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: The test suite takes twelve minutes because every class starts its own context

**Scenario.** A service has 60 integration test classes. Each class declares its own `@MockitoBean` set or `@TestPropertySource`, and the pipeline spends most of its time starting the application.

**Symptoms.** The log shows the Spring banner dozens of times; the Surefire report lists per-class times of five to nine seconds for the first test and milliseconds for the rest; JVM memory grows during the run because up to 32 contexts stay alive.

**Diagnosis.** (1) Count banners: `grep -c "Started .* in" target/surefire-reports/*-output.txt`. (2) Enable the cache logger shown above and compare the `misses` figure with the number of classes. (3) For two classes that should share a context, print the differences: unequal `@MockitoBean` sets, `@ActiveProfiles` order, `@TestPropertySource` values, `@Import` lists and `@DirtiesContext` usage are the usual causes.

**Root cause.** The cache key includes every configuration element, so cosmetic differences (a property set in one class only, a mock declared in one class only) create separate contexts. `@DirtiesContext` discards the context after the class or method, forcing a rebuild.

**Fix.** Move shared declarations to an abstract base class or a meta-annotation so that all classes present an identical key; declare mocks needed by few tests on a `@TestConfiguration`-free slice instead of the full context; replace `@DirtiesContext` with explicit cleanup (truncate tables, reset a fake) wherever possible. Where a few tests need distinct configuration, group them in a separate Failsafe execution so the common contexts are not evicted.

blocks.title: AbstractIntegrationTest.java

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Track the number of context start-ups per build as a metric; fail the build when it exceeds an agreed budget (for example five). Prefer slices to `@SpringBootTest` for new tests.

#### Problem 2: A web slice test fails at start-up with a missing bean

**Scenario.** A new `@WebMvcTest` for a controller fails immediately after a developer adds a second dependency (`AuditService`) to the controller constructor.

**Symptoms.** `UnsatisfiedDependencyException: Error creating bean with name 'orderController' ... No` `qualifying bean of type 'shop.audit.AuditService'`.

**Diagnosis.** Read the innermost cause in the trace; it names the type. Confirm that the type is a `@Service` or `@Component`, which a web slice never scans.

**Root cause.** Slices include only the stereotypes of their layer. The new collaborator is outside the slice.

**Fix.** Declare `@MockitoBean AuditService audit;` in the test. If the collaborator is configuration-heavy and not mockable (for example a `Clock` or `PasswordEncoder` bean), supply it through `@Import(TestBeans.class)` or a nested `@TestConfiguration` class. Do not switch to `@SpringBootTest` to avoid the error: that hides the dependency and slows the test.

**Prevention.** Keep controllers thin so that their dependency list stays short; a controller with five collaborators is a design signal.

#### Problem 3: A mock is injected into the wrong place, or the test sees the real bean

**Scenario.** A test declares `@MockitoBean PaymentClient client` but the service under test still calls the real HTTP client, or two beans of the same type exist and the wrong one is replaced.

**Symptoms.** Real network calls from tests, or a mock that is never invoked (`Wanted but not invoked`).

**Diagnosis.** (1) Check whether the production code constructs the collaborator with `new` rather than receiving it from the container; a mock cannot replace an object that is not a bean. (2) List bean definitions of the type: `ctx.getBeanNamesForType(PaymentClient.class)`. (3) With two candidates, `@MockitoBean` without a name fails on ambiguity or replaces the primary candidate, depending on the version.

**Root cause.** Bean override works on the application context only. Objects created with `new`, static factories and singletons outside Spring are invisible to it.

**Fix.** Obtain collaborators through constructor injection; when two beans exist, name the one to replace: `@MockitoBean(name = "primaryPaymentClient")`.

**Prevention.** Forbid `new` for infrastructure collaborators in services; the design that makes mocking possible is the same design that makes the class testable without Spring.

#### Problem 4: Tests alter each other through a shared cached context

**Scenario.** A test class changes a singleton bean (for example, sets a feature flag in an in-memory holder) and the next class, sharing the cached context, fails.

**Symptoms.** Order-dependent failures that disappear when the class runs alone.

**Diagnosis.** Run the two classes in both orders. Search for tests that mutate bean state (`ReflectionTestUtils.setField`, `holder.set(...)`, caches filled by the test).

**Root cause.** A cached context shares singleton beans across all classes that use it; state in those beans persists. **Fix.** Reset state in `@AfterEach`, or prefer `@DirtiesContext` only for the one class that cannot clean up. Cache and holder beans should expose a reset method for tests, or the test should use a fresh instance supplied through `@TestConfiguration`.

**Prevention.** Treat singleton beans in tests as shared infrastructure: tests may read them freely and must restore any change they make.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between @SpringBootTest and @WebMvcTest?

`@SpringBootTest` starts the whole application context (optionally with a real server). `@WebMvcTest` starts only the MVC layer: controllers, advice, converters, filters and MVC auto-configuration, with collaborators supplied as mocks. The slice is faster and checks only web behaviour.

#### How does the test context cache work and what invalidates it?

The `TestContext` framework caches started contexts in a map keyed by the merged context configuration (classes, profiles, properties, customizers such as mock declarations). A different key produces a new context. `@DirtiesContext` removes the context from the cache. The default capacity is 32 contexts with LRU eviction.

#### Why can @MockitoBean slow down a test suite?

Each distinct set of declared overrides is part of the cache key. Tests that declare different mocks cannot share a context, so each combination costs one context start-up.

#### What does MockMvc test, and what does it not test?

It tests everything inside the DispatcherServlet pipeline: filters, mapping, binding, validation, conversion and exception handling. It does not start a servlet container, so error pages, container configuration, compression and real HTTP behaviour are untested.

#### Why are flush() and clear() needed in a repository test?

Writes are buffered in the persistence context until a flush, and reads are served from its first-level cache. Without flush and clear, the test verifies the cache rather than the SQL and the mapping.

#### How is a controller secured in a slice test?

`@WebMvcTest` includes Spring Security; tests use `@WithMockUser` or the `jwt()` request post-processor from `spring-security-test`, and `csrf()` for state-changing requests. Custom `SecurityFilterChain` beans must be imported with `@Import`, because configuration classes are outside the scan filter.

#### What replaced @MockBean?

`@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean` from Spring Framework 6.2 (usable from Boot 3.4). The older annotations are deprecated.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A slice test starts one layer: web, persistence, JSON or HTTP client. Everything else is mocked or imported explicitly.
- The context cache key is the full merged configuration; a different mock set, property or profile means a new context start-up.
- Reduce distinct configurations with a shared base class or meta-annotation, and avoid `@DirtiesContext` unless state cannot be reset.
- `@MockitoBean` replaces `@MockBean` from Boot 3.4; mocks only replace beans, not objects created with `new`.
- MockMvc exercises the whole MVC pipeline without a server; use a random-port test when container behaviour matters.
- In repository tests, flush and clear the persistence context before asserting, and use the production database engine.

An integration test verifies that the application works together with the systems it depends on: the relational database with its real SQL dialect and constraints, the message broker with its real delivery semantics, the cache with its real eviction behaviour. Embedded substitutes (H2 for PostgreSQL, an in-memory fake for Kafka) are fast but differ in exactly the places where production defects occur. Testcontainers closes this gap by starting the real software in a throw-away Docker container from inside the test run. Spring Boot 3.1 added first-class support (`@ServiceConnection`), so that a container replaces connection properties without manual wiring. This chapter covers the mechanism, the configuration patterns that keep a suite fast, stubbing of HTTP dependencies, contract testing and security tests.

### Concept and mechanism

#### How Testcontainers works

Testcontainers is a Java library that talks to the Docker Engine API through the socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`, or `DOCKER_HOST`). For each `GenericContainer` or specialised subclass (`PostgreSQLContainer`, `KafkaContainer`) the library performs these steps.

1. Pulls the image if absent (the first run on a build agent can take a minute).
2. Creates and starts the container with a random host port mapped to each exposed container port, which avoids port conflicts between parallel builds.
3. Evaluates a **wait strategy** until the service is ready: a log line (`Wait.forLogMessage`), a listening port, an HTTP endpoint or a health check. A container whose process has started is not necessarily ready; the wait strategy is the readiness contract.
4. Exposes the mapped host, port and credentials (`getJdbcUrl()`, `getBootstrapServers()`).
5. Registers the container with **Ryuk**, a sidecar container that deletes containers, networks and volumes created by the JVM when the JVM exits, even after a crash.

blocks.text:
#### Wiring the container into Spring Boot

Three mechanisms exist, in decreasing order of preference.

`@ServiceConnection` (Boot 3.1 and later; package `org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection`). Annotating a container field or `@Bean` method makes Boot create a `ConnectionDetails` bean (for example `JdbcConnectionDetails`, `KafkaConnectionDetails`) that the auto-configuration uses instead of the property values. No property names appear in the test, so the test remains valid when property names change. Supported types include `PostgreSQLContainer`, `MySQLContainer`, `KafkaContainer`, `MongoDBContainer`, `RedisContainer`; a plain `GenericContainer` needs `@ServiceConnection(name = "redis")` so Boot can determine the service. The dependency `spring-boot-testcontainers` is required (test scope).

`@DynamicPropertySource` registers properties computed after the container starts. It is more verbose and works for any container and any property, including application-specific ones.

`@ImportTestcontainers` imports container declarations from an interface, which allows one declaration to be shared by many test classes and by the development-time launcher.

A container declared as a `static` field with the Jupiter `@Container` annotation is started before the first test of the class and stopped after the last. Container beans (`@Bean @ServiceConnection PostgreSQLContainer<?>`) are managed by the Spring context instead: they start with the context and stop with it, which matches the context cache lifetime and avoids a stopped container behind a cached context.

#### The singleton container pattern

Starting a PostgreSQL container takes two to five seconds. A container per test class multiplies that cost by the number of classes. The singleton pattern starts one container per JVM, in a shared holder, and shares it among all classes; tests isolate themselves through unique data or by truncating tables.

blocks.title: Containers.java

blocks.text:
Because the container is a bean of a configuration that is imported by the shared base class, every subclass presents the same context key and therefore the same container. The two optimisations compose: one cached context and one container.

### Worked example

The example verifies an order repository, a Flyway migration and the HTTP endpoint against real PostgreSQL, a Kafka producer against a real broker, and an outgoing payment call against a stub.

#### Shared base class

blocks.title: AbstractIntegrationTest.java

blocks.text: #### Database, migration and endpoint

blocks.title: OrderApiIT.java

blocks.text:
Because the server runs in its own thread, a `@Transactional` test method does **not** roll back what the server wrote (the HTTP handler uses a different connection and transaction). Cleanup is therefore explicit: `TRUNCATE ... RESTART` `IDENTITY CASCADE` in `@BeforeEach`.

#### Kafka with a real broker

blocks.title: ShipmentPublisherIT.java

blocks.text:
The assertion on the **key** matters: partition assignment follows the key, so ordering guarantees depend on it. A mocked `KafkaTemplate` would never reveal a wrong key. The Kafka container class and image name depend on the Testcontainers version (`org.testcontainers.containers.KafkaContainer` accepts `apache/kafka` images from Testcontainers 1.20; older versions use `confluentinc/cp-kafka`); the version in the build file governs.

#### Stubbing an HTTP dependency

Calls to third-party HTTP services are not made in tests. WireMock runs an HTTP server inside the test JVM (or in a container) and answers from declared stubs, including delays and fault injection. `@AutoConfigureWireMock(port = 0)` from Spring Cloud Contract WireMock starts it on a random port and exposes it as the property `wiremock.server.port`.

blocks.title: PaymentClientWireMockIT.java

blocks.text: The mechanism of such a stub is small enough to reproduce with the JDK's built-in `com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer`. The program below serves three scripted responses (slow, then 503, then 200) and calls them with a client whose per-request timeout is 150 ms; it demonstrates what a timeout test and a fault-injection test verify. The server uses a four-thread executor: with the default single-threaded dispatcher the slow first response blocks the later ones, which is a frequent source of misleading timeouts in hand-made stubs.

$ java StubServerDemo.java

call 2 -> 503 {"error":"unavailable"} [106 ms]
call 3 -> 200 {"status":"OK"} [51 ms]

blocks.text:
#### Contract testing and security tests

When two services are developed by different teams, a stub written by the consumer may drift from the real provider. **Consumer-driven contract testing** records the interactions the consumer relies on as a contract; the provider build verifies that it satisfies every contract, and the consumer build receives stubs generated from the same contract. Two toolchains are common: Spring Cloud Contract (contracts in a Groovy, YAML or Kotlin DSL, provider tests generated automatically, stubs published as a `-stubs` jar and consumed through `@AutoConfigureStubRunner`) and Pact (language-neutral JSON pacts exchanged through a broker). Both detect a breaking change in a provider (a renamed field, a removed status) in the provider's build, before deployment. They complement, and do not replace, a small number of end-to-end checks.

Security rules are verified by requests with a security context. `spring-security-test` supplies `@WithMockUser(roles` `= "ADMIN")`, `SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt()` for resource servers and `csrf()` for form-based applications. A test suite for protected endpoints asserts three outcomes per endpoint: anonymous is rejected (`401`), authenticated without the right authority is forbidden (`403`), authorised succeeds.

### Hands-on

Container-based tests need a reachable Docker daemon. On a developer machine, any Docker-compatible runtime works; on CI the choice affects speed and configuration (see the problems below). The command line does not change:

blocks.text:
Container reuse speeds up the local edit-run loop. It requires both `withReuse(true)` on the container and `testcontainers.reuse.enable=true` in `~/.testcontainers.properties`; reused containers are not removed by Ryuk and carry state between runs, so it is a developer convenience and is not enabled in CI. Spring Boot's development-time support (`SpringApplication.from(Application::main).with(Containers.class).run(args)`, with `@RestartScope` on container beans) shares the same container declarations for local runs.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: Tests pass against H2 and fail against PostgreSQL in production

**Scenario.** Repository tests run on an in-memory H2 database (the default replacement of `@DataJpaTest`) and are green. After deployment, a query using a PostgreSQL operator fails, and a duplicate insert leaves a request in a broken state.

**Symptoms.** `PSQLException: ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of` `transaction block` in production logs; a native query with `->>` or `ILIKE` that cannot even be prepared on H2; `jsonb` columns that the H2-based schema generation silently maps differently.

**Diagnosis.** Compare the dialects. The statements below were executed on a real PostgreSQL 16 server and show behaviour that an embedded database must emulate.

blocks.title: dialect_check.sql

blocks.code:
$ psql -f dialect_check.sql
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
INSERT 0 1
   name
----------
 Keyboard
(1 row)

   name
----------
 Keyboard
(1 row)

BEGIN
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "product_name_key"
DETAIL:  Key (name)=(Mouse) already exists.
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
ROLLBACK
 name
------
(0 rows)
blocks.title: Real output from PostgreSQL 16

blocks.text:
Three facts follow. The `jsonb` type, the `->>` operator and `ILIKE` are PostgreSQL features; an embedded engine supports them only partially or through a compatibility mode. The `LIKE` comparison is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL (zero rows for `'key%'`), whereas other engines or collations may be case-insensitive. After a failed statement inside a transaction, PostgreSQL rejects every further statement until rollback; code that catches a constraint violation and continues inside the same transaction works on engines that do not abort the transaction and fails on PostgreSQL. (The H2-side behaviour was not executed on the build machine; it is stated from the H2 documentation, and the version in use should be checked.)

**Root cause.** The test database is not the production database; the compatibility mode (`MODE=PostgreSQL`) emulates a subset only.

**Fix.** Use the production engine in tests: Testcontainers with the same major version as production (`postgres:16`). Run the real Flyway migrations rather than `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create`, so that migration scripts are tested too. Catch constraint violations in a separate transaction (`REQUIRES_NEW`) or avoid catching them.

**Prevention.** Ban H2 in the test classpath by a dependency rule; keep the container image version in one place (a constant or the `Containers` configuration) and update it together with production.

blocks.text:
**Problem 2: The pipeline fails randomly with "Connection refused" while starting containers** **Scenario.** On a shared CI runner, one build in ten fails with `Connection to localhost:49153 refused` or `Could not` `connect to Ryuk`, and with an authentication error against the database in the first test.

**Symptoms.** The failure occurs in the first test that touches the database; re-running the job succeeds. Slow runners fail more often. **Diagnosis.** (1) Read the container log in the build output (`Container postgres:16-alpine started in PT...`): a start time near the wait timeout indicates an overloaded runner. (2) Check whether the wait strategy is satisfied by the wrong event. PostgreSQL logs "database system is ready to accept connections" twice during initialisation; a wait strategy that matches only one occurrence is satisfied while the init script is still running. The official `PostgreSQLContainer` waits for two occurrences. A hand-written `GenericContainer` for a database needs the same care. (3) On Docker-in-Docker runners, check that the host name used to reach mapped ports is correct (`TESTCONTAINERS_HOST_OVERRIDE`).

**Root cause.** The test starts before the service is ready, because the wait strategy is missing, wrong, or its timeout is shorter than the container start time under load.

**Fix.** Use the specialised container class, or define an explicit strategy and timeout:

blocks.title: Waits.java

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Pre-pull images in the runner image or a registry mirror; cap parallel jobs per runner; use a CI service that offers a Docker daemon with enough memory (databases and brokers need 1 GB or more each); keep one container per JVM rather than per class.

#### Problem 3: Integration tests leave data behind and fail in a different order

**Scenario.** Two integration tests pass individually. Run together, the second fails with a unique-key violation or an unexpected row count.

**Symptoms.** Failures depend on class order; a test that asserts `count == 1` returns 2.

**Diagnosis.** Check whether the failing test is `@Transactional`: on `RANDOM_PORT` tests the server transaction commits, so rollback does not apply. Query the table after the first test to see the leftovers.

**Root cause.** The data written through the HTTP layer commits; the test's own transaction cannot undo it.

**Fix.** Clean explicitly before each test (`TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE`), or give each test unique keys (random SKU, unique e-mail) and assert on those only. For `MOCK` web environment tests, in-process calls share the test transaction and rollback works.

**Prevention.** Decide on one isolation strategy per suite and document it in the base class; do not mix transactional rollback and explicit cleanup in the same suite.

#### Problem 4: Outgoing HTTP calls reach a real third-party service from CI

**Scenario.** A test of the checkout flow calls the real payment sandbox and fails whenever the sandbox is slow or rate-limited.

**Symptoms.** Failures coincide with external outages; the log shows real host names; builds fail for network-restricted runners.

**Diagnosis.** Check the effective property `payment.base-url` in the test context (`/actuator/env` in a running test, or a debug assertion on the `Environment`). Search the test classpath for production URLs in `application.yml`.

**Root cause.** The test profile does not override the client base URL, so the production-default URL is used.

**Fix.** Point the URL to a WireMock instance (`@AutoConfigureWireMock`) and simulate faults (delay, 503, malformed body) as shown above. Block accidental outbound traffic by setting the default URL in `application-test.properties` to an unroutable address (`http://localhost:1`), which converts a missing override into an immediate failure.

**Prevention.** Keep third-party base URLs out of defaults; add a contract test so that the stubs track the real provider.

### Questions to expect

#### Why use Testcontainers instead of H2?

The embedded database differs from the production database in types, operators, SQL functions, locking and transaction semantics, so tests can pass for wrong reasons. A container runs the real engine and version, and also verifies the migration scripts.

#### What does @ServiceConnection do?

It creates a `ConnectionDetails` bean from the running container so that the auto-configuration connects to it, replacing connection properties. The test needs no property names and stays correct when the container port is random.

#### How is container start-up cost controlled?

One container per JVM (singleton or bean-scoped container imported by a shared base class), a shared cached context, images pre-pulled on the runner, and optional reuse in local development.

#### Why does @Transactional not roll back in a RANDOM_PORT test?

The client and the server handle the request on different threads and connections, so the server's transaction commits independently of the test's transaction.

#### What is Ryuk?

A Testcontainers sidecar that removes containers, networks and volumes created by a test JVM when the JVM terminates, including after a crash.

#### What is the benefit of consumer-driven contracts?

The provider build fails when it breaks an expectation of any consumer, and consumers test against stubs generated from the same contract, so stubs cannot drift from reality.

#### When is WireMock preferable to MockRestServiceServer?

WireMock exercises the complete HTTP stack, including timeouts, connection handling, serialisation and fault injection. `MockRestServiceServer` replaces the request factory, so it verifies mapping logic quickly but not network behaviour.

#### How are authorisation rules tested?

With request post-processors or annotations from `spring-security-test`, asserting `401` for anonymous, `403` for insufficient authority and success for an authorised principal.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Embedded databases hide dialect, type and transaction differences; use the production engine through Testcontainers and run the real migrations.
- `@ServiceConnection` wires a container into auto-configuration without property names; container beans share the lifetime of the cached context.
- Keep suites fast: one container per JVM, one cached context, images pre-pulled, explicit data cleanup for server-side commits.
- Wait strategies define readiness; a container that has started is not necessarily ready.
- Stub HTTP dependencies with WireMock, including delays and faults, and protect the build against accidental real calls.
- Contract tests keep stubs and providers in agreement; security tests assert 401, 403 and success per endpoint.

An application that passes its tests can still fail in production, and the first question during an incident is always the same: what is the system doing now? Spring Boot Actuator answers it with operational endpoints (health, metrics, thread dumps, environment), and Micrometer provides the vendor-neutral metrics API on which those answers are built. Together they implement the first two pillars of observability, health and metrics. (Logs and traces are treated in the chapter on logging and in the Microservices part.) This chapter explains the internals of both, shows the instrumentation of application code, and develops the operational methods (RED, USE, alerting) that turn raw numbers into decisions.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Endpoints, exposure and access

An Actuator endpoint is a bean annotated `@Endpoint` whose methods (`@ReadOperation`, `@WriteOperation`, `@DeleteOperation`) are technology-neutral. Adapters expose the same operation over JMX and over HTTP (`WebMvcEndpointHandlerMapping` under the base path `/actuator`). Two independent controls decide whether an endpoint is reachable: **exposure** selects the endpoints published on a technology, and **access** (Boot 3.4 and later: `management.endpoint.<id>.access`, previously `enabled`) selects what operations are permitted at all. By default only `health` is exposed over HTTP and JMX. Exposing everything is a one-line change that must never reach production unreviewed, because `env`, `heapdump`, `threaddump` and `beans` disclose secrets, memory contents and internal structure.

rows: Aggregated status of dependencies; probe groups for Kubernetes
Names and values of recorded meters (`/actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used`)
All meters in Prometheus text format (needs `micrometer-registry-prometheus`)
Read and change log levels at run time
Properties of the environment; values sanitised by default
Stack of every thread (same content as `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`)
HPROF heap dump; access disabled by default
Last 100 HTTP exchanges; needs an `HttpExchangeRepository` bean (name changed from `httptrace` in Boot 3)
blocks.caption: Frequently used endpoints (Boot 3.5).

blocks.text: Production practice has three parts: expose the minimum (`health`, `info`, `prometheus`, optionally `loggers`), move the management endpoints to a separate port that is not routed by the public ingress (`management.server.port=9090`), and protect what remains with Spring Security (`EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint()` in a dedicated `SecurityFilterChain`).

blocks.text:
#### Health: indicators, groups and probes

`HealthEndpoint` aggregates `HealthIndicator` beans (database, disk space, Redis, Kafka and custom ones) through a `StatusAggregator`. The default order is `DOWN`, `OUT_OF_SERVICE`, `UP`, `UNKNOWN`: any `DOWN` indicator makes the aggregate `DOWN`, which the HTTP adapter maps to status code 503. Details (`components`) are shown according to `management.endpoint.health.show-details` (`never` by default; `when-authorized` or `always`).

**Health groups** select subsets of indicators under their own path (`management.endpoint.health.group.<name>.include`). Boot defines two groups for Kubernetes probes, available as `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` when `management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true` (enabled automatically when Boot detects a Kubernetes environment). The groups are backed by `ApplicationAvailability`, which holds two states: `LivenessState` (`CORRECT` or `BROKEN`) and `ReadinessState` (`ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC` or `REFUSING_TRAFFIC`). The application changes them by publishing an `AvailabilityChangeEvent`; Boot itself switches readiness on after startup and off when graceful shutdown begins.

The two probes answer different questions, and confusing them is the most common probe defect:

- **Liveness** asks whether the process is irrecoverably broken and must be restarted. A failing liveness probe causes the kubelet to kill the container. It must therefore depend on nothing outside the process: a database outage is not cured by restarting the application, and restarting every replica at once converts a partial outage into a total one.
- **Readiness** asks whether the instance can serve requests now. A failing readiness probe removes the pod from the Service endpoints without restarting it. It may include essential dependencies, and it is the correct place to express "warming up" or "draining".
- **Startup probe** gives slow-starting applications a separate, generous budget before liveness checking begins.

blocks.text:
#### Micrometer: meters, registries and tags

Micrometer is to metrics what SLF4J is to logging: an API in front of many monitoring systems. A `MeterRegistry` creates and stores **meters**; each meter is identified by a name and a set of key-value **tags**. Boot configures a `CompositeMeterRegistry` containing one registry per dependency present on the classpath (`PrometheusMeterRegistry`, `OtlpMeterRegistry`, and so on) and binds a large set of `MeterBinder` beans: JVM memory and GC, threads, class loading, process CPU, Tomcat, HikariCP, logback event counts, `http.server.requests`, `http.client.requests`, cache statistics.

blocks.text:
In Boot 3, instrumentation is unified under the **Observation API** (`ObservationRegistry`, `Observation`, `@Observed`): one instrumented block yields a timer metric and, when a tracer is present, a span with the same name and tags. `http.server.requests`, `http.client.requests`, `spring.data.repository.invocations` and `spring.security.*` are observations.

#### Tags and cardinality

Each distinct combination of tag values is a separate **time series** that the monitoring system stores and indexes. The series count of a metric is the product of the numbers of values of its tags, multiplied by the number of histogram buckets. Tags with unbounded values (user ID, order ID, raw URL, exception message, e-mail address) therefore create an unbounded number of series, exhaust memory in the metrics backend and in the application (the registry keeps every meter), and are the standard cause of "Prometheus out of memory" incidents. Spring MVC avoids the problem for URLs by tagging with the **template** (`/orders/{id}`) rather than the actual path; custom code must follow the same rule.

#### The Prometheus format and the pull model

Prometheus **pulls**: it requests `/actuator/prometheus` every scrape interval (commonly 15 s) from every instance, stores each sample with a timestamp and evaluates queries and alert rules on the stored series. Counters are cumulative; rates are computed at query time (`rate(x[5m])`). A latency histogram is exposed as cumulative bucket counters (`..._bucket{le="0.1"}`) plus `_sum` and `_count`; quantiles are estimated at query time with `histogram_quantile`, which allows aggregation across instances (percentiles pre-computed inside the application cannot be averaged correctly across instances).

The program below implements the core of a histogram and its exposition in plain Java. It records 2000 synthetic latencies (96 percent between 15 and 60 ms, 4 percent between 800 and 1200 ms), prints the mean and the quantiles computed exactly and from buckets, writes the result in Prometheus text format, and computes series counts for templated and raw URIs.

blocks.text: What to notice: the mean (78.0 ms) hides that 4 percent of requests take about a second; the median is 39 ms. The bucket-based p99 estimate (1802 ms) differs from the exact value (1119 ms) because the only bucket boundaries around the answer are 1000 ms and 2500 ms, and interpolation assumes a uniform spread inside the bucket: **the** **accuracy of a histogram quantile is bounded by the bucket layout**, so boundaries must be placed around the service-level objective (for example 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 ms). Finally, replacing a templated URI by raw URIs multiplies the series count by 4000.

blocks.text:
#### Operational methods: RED, USE and alerting

Dashboards and alerts are organised around two checklists. The **RED method** applies to every request-serving component: **R**ate (requests per second), **E**rrors (failed requests per second or as a ratio) and **D**uration (latency distribution). The **USE method** applies to resources (CPU, memory, connection pool, thread pool, disk): **U**tilisation (fraction of capacity in use), **S**aturation (queued or waiting work) and **E**rrors. In a Spring Boot service, RED comes from `http.server.requests`; USE comes from `hikaricp.connections.*` (active, pending, timeouts), `tomcat.threads.*` (busy against configured), `jvm.memory.*`, `jvm.gc.pause` and `executor.*` for `@Async` pools.

Alerts should fire on symptoms users experience (error ratio, latency of the slow tail, saturation that precedes failure), not on every internal cause (CPU at 80 percent). A rule has an expression, a duration (`for`) that filters brief spikes, a severity label and a link to a runbook.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

The service from the earlier chapters exposes an order API. The requirements: Kubernetes probes that behave correctly, business and latency metrics, a health indicator for a non-critical dependency, management endpoints on a separate port with restricted access, and a Prometheus scrape plus two alert rules.

#### Configuration

blocks.code:
management:
  server:
    port: 9090                       # not published by the public Ingress
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus,loggers
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true                # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness
      show-details: when-authorized
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState,db,inventory
        liveness:
          include: livenessState     # nothing external in liveness
    loggers:
      access: read-only              # Boot 3.4+: no level changes from outside
  metrics:
    tags:
      application: ${spring.application.name}
    distribution:
      percentiles-histogram:
        http.server.requests: true
      slo:
        http.server.requests: 50ms,100ms,200ms,500ms,1s
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
server:
  shutdown: graceful
  tomcat:
    mbeanregistry:
      enabled: true                  # exposes tomcat.threads.* meters
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text:
The `slo` entry makes the histogram buckets coincide with the latency objectives, which fixes the quantile-accuracy problem shown above. The Tomcat setting is required because Tomcat meters are disabled by default.

#### Custom metrics

blocks.title: OrderMetrics.java

blocks.text:
Counters and timers are created once in the constructor and reused. Creating a meter by name on every call (`registry.counter("orders.rejected", "reason", reason)`) is permitted and cheap enough for bounded tags, but a dynamic tag value must come from a closed set.

#### Custom health indicator

blocks.title: InventoryHealthIndicator.java

blocks.text:
The bean name `inventory` becomes the component key (the suffix `HealthIndicator` is stripped from the default name). It is listed in the readiness group above, so an unreachable inventory service removes the pod from rotation without restarting it.

#### Securing the management port

blocks.title: ManagementSecurityConfig.java

blocks.text:
Probes and the Prometheus scrape must authenticate or be network-restricted. Where the management port is reachable only inside the cluster, a network policy replaces the credentials for `health` and `prometheus`; the `OPS` role then guards `loggers` and the rest.

#### Prometheus scrape and alert rules

blocks.code:
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
rule_files:
  - alerts.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: order-service
    metrics_path: /actuator/prometheus
    kubernetes_sd_configs:
      - role: pod
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app]
        regex: order-service
        action: keep
      - source_labels: [__address__]
        regex: '([^:]+)(?::\d+)?'
        replacement: '$1:9090'
        target_label: __address__
blocks.title: prometheus.yml

blocks.code:
groups:
  - name: order-service
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRatio
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) > 0.02
        for: 10m
        labels: {severity: page}
        annotations:
          summary: "More than 2% of requests fail for 10 minutes"
      - alert: SlowTail
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.99,
            sum by (le) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m])))
          > 0.5
        for: 10m
        labels: {severity: ticket}
        annotations:
          summary: "p99 latency above 500 ms for 10 minutes"
      - alert: HikariPoolSaturated
        expr: max(hikaricp_connections_pending{application="order-service"}) > 0
        for: 5m
        labels: {severity: ticket}
blocks.title: alerts.yml

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

With the configuration above, the endpoints behave as follows. The output is typical of Boot 3.4 and was not produced on the build machine.

blocks.code:
$ curl -s localhost:9090/actuator/health/readiness
{"status":"UP","components":{"db":{"status":"UP"},"inventory":{"status":"UP"},
"readinessState":{"status":"UP"}}}
$ curl -s localhost:9090/actuator/metrics/http.server.requests | head -c 300
{"name":"http.server.requests","baseUnit":"seconds","measurements":[
{"statistic":"COUNT","value":1842.0},{"statistic":"TOTAL_TIME","value":96.4},
{"statistic":"MAX","value":1.21}],"availableTags":[{"tag":"uri","values":["/orders/{id}"]},...
$ curl -s localhost:9090/actuator/prometheus \
    | grep -E '^(orders_placed|tomcat_threads_busy|hikaricp_connections_active)'
orders_placed_total{application="order-service"} 311.0
tomcat_threads_busy_threads{application="order-service",name="http-nio-8080"} 4.0
hikaricp_connections_active{application="order-service",pool="HikariPool-1"} 2.0
blocks.title: Typical output (not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
Two naming details matter when writing queries. Micrometer names such as `orders.placed` become `orders_placed_total` for counters and `http_server_requests_seconds_*` for timers in Prometheus, because the exporter converts dots to underscores and appends base units. A query written against the Micrometer name returns no data.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: The readiness probe fails during start-up and the rollout stalls

**Scenario.** A new version is deployed with a rolling update. The new pods stay `0/1 Ready`, the old pods are not replaced, and the deployment reports `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.

**Symptoms.** `kubectl get pods` shows `Running 0/1`; `kubectl describe pod` lists `Readiness probe failed: HTTP` `probe failed with statuscode: 503`. The application log shows a normal start.

**Diagnosis.** (1) Query the probe from inside the pod: `kubectl exec <pod> -- wget -qO-` `localhost:9090/actuator/health/readiness`. (2) Show details by temporarily setting `management.endpoint.health.show-details=always` or reading the log of the health aggregation. (3) Identify the failing component; with the configuration above it is typically `db` (wrong credentials from the new secret) or `inventory` (network policy blocks the call). (4) Check whether the probe port matches `management.server.port` (a probe sent to 8080 receives 404 or 401 when the management port moved).

**Root cause.** Readiness includes a dependency that is unreachable from the new pod, or the probe is aimed at the wrong port or path. The platform behaves correctly: it does not route traffic to an instance that reports itself unable to serve, and the rolling update waits for readiness.

**Fix.** Correct the dependency (secret, network policy) or the probe definition:

blocks.code:
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090}
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
  timeoutSeconds: 2
blocks.title: deployment.yaml

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Run the readiness endpoint in the integration test suite against the Testcontainers database, so a broken connection configuration fails the build rather than the rollout. Keep non-essential dependencies out of the readiness group so that their outage degrades a feature rather than removing every pod.

#### Problem 2: The liveness probe kills a healthy but slow pod, repeatedly

**Scenario.** After a feature adds cache warming, start-up grows from 20 s to 45 s. The pods enter a restart loop in Kubernetes while the same image runs normally on a developer machine.

**Symptoms.** `RESTARTS` increases every 20 to 30 seconds, `kubectl describe pod` shows `Liveness probe failed` and `Container ... failed liveness probe, will be restarted`. The application log ends abruptly during start-up, repeated each time.

**Diagnosis.** Compare the time to first successful response with the probe schedule. The following model reproduces the kubelet logic in virtual time (probes start after `initialDelay`, every `period`, restart after `failureThreshold` consecutive failures; the real kubelet also applies restart back-off, which is omitted).

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The liveness probe begins at 10 s and tolerates 3 failures at a 5 s period, so the container is killed at 20 s, before the 45 s start-up completes. Every restart repeats the same sequence.

**Fix.** Add a startup probe whose budget (`periodSeconds` x `failureThreshold`) exceeds the worst-case start-up time, and keep the liveness probe strict afterwards:

blocks.code:
startupProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090}
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 24          # up to 120 s to start
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090}
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
blocks.title: deployment.yaml

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Measure start-up in the cluster (the `application.started.time` and `application.ready.time` metrics) rather than locally, and size the startup budget from the 99th percentile. Never include the database or other remote services in liveness: a shared outage would restart every replica simultaneously.

#### Problem 3: The metrics backend runs out of memory after a release (cardinality explosion)

**Scenario.** A developer adds a timer tagged with the customer identifier to analyse slow customers. Within hours the Prometheus server is OOM-killed and dashboards are empty.

**Symptoms.** `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` grows from 60,000 to several million; scrape duration climbs; the response of `/actuator/prometheus` grows from kilobytes to hundreds of megabytes; the application heap grows because the registry retains every meter.

**Diagnosis.** (1) Rank metrics by series count in Prometheus: `topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))`. (2) Inspect the label values of the top metric: `count(count by (customerId) (orders_payment_seconds_count))`. (3) Compare with the application's metric list at `/actuator/metrics` and read the tag values at `/actuator/metrics/orders.payment`.

**Root cause.** The tag has an unbounded value set. The series count is the product of tag value counts times the bucket count; the arithmetic computed by the program above shows 66,000 series for 25 templated URIs and 264 million for 100,000 raw URIs.

**Fix.** Remove the tag; record the high-cardinality identifier in logs or trace attributes, where cost scales with events and not with distinct values. As a protection, add a registry filter that caps tag values and denies offenders:

blocks.title: MeterGuardConfig.java

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Review every new tag during code review with the question "how many distinct values can this have in a year?". Alert on `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` growth and on scrape sample counts (`scrape_samples_scraped`) per job.

#### Problem 4: Latency percentiles are missing or wrong in the dashboard

**Scenario.** A dashboard panel shows "average latency 80 ms" while customers complain about slow checkouts. The query for p99 returns "no data".

**Symptoms.** `http_server_requests_seconds_bucket` does not exist in Prometheus; only `_count`, `_sum` and `_max` exist. A p99 panel based on `histogram_quantile` is empty.

**Diagnosis.** `curl localhost:9090/actuator/prometheus | grep http_server_requests_seconds_bucket | head`. If nothing is printed, histogram publishing is off, which is the default for `http.server.requests`.

**Root cause.** Boot publishes only count, total time and max for server requests unless a distribution is requested. An average computed from `_sum / _count` hides the slow tail (78.0 ms mean against a 1.12 s p99 in the program above).

**Fix.** Enable the histogram and align the buckets with the objectives (configuration shown in the worked example), then query `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m])))`. Do not use client-side percentiles (`management.metrics.distribution.percentiles`) for dashboards across several instances, because pre-computed quantiles cannot be aggregated.

**Prevention.** Define latency objectives per endpoint group and verify during review that the bucket boundaries bracket them. Show p50, p95 and p99 together with the request rate.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between liveness and readiness probes?

Liveness reports whether the process must be restarted; a failure makes the kubelet kill the container. Readiness reports whether the instance can accept traffic; a failure removes it from the Service endpoints without a restart. Liveness must not depend on external systems; readiness may.

#### How does Spring Boot compute the aggregate health status?

`HealthEndpoint` collects the status of every `HealthIndicator` in the group and a `StatusAggregator` chooses the most severe by the order `DOWN`, `OUT_OF_SERVICE`, `UP`, `UNKNOWN`. `DOWN` is returned as HTTP 503.

#### How are Actuator endpoints secured in production?

Expose the minimum set, move them to a separate management port that is not routed publicly, restrict access with a `SecurityFilterChain` using `EndpointRequest`, keep sanitised values (`show-values=never`), and disable `heapdump` and `env` unless operationally required.

#### What is metric cardinality and why does it matter?

It is the number of distinct time series, the product of tag value counts times the number of buckets. Unbounded tag values (identifiers, raw URLs) multiply storage and memory in the application and in the backend until it fails.

#### Counter, gauge, timer: which is used for what?

A counter counts events and only increases; a gauge samples a current value that can rise and fall; a timer records the count and duration of events, optionally with a histogram.

#### Why are histograms preferred to pre-computed percentiles?

Bucket counts can be summed across instances and time windows, and the quantile is computed afterwards; pre-computed percentiles cannot be combined correctly.

#### What do RED and USE stand for?

RED (rate, errors, duration) describes the requests a service handles; USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) describes the resources it consumes.

#### Which metrics reveal thread pool or connection pool saturation?

`tomcat.threads.busy` approaching `tomcat.threads.config.max`, `hikaricp.connections.pending` above zero, `hikaricp.connections.timeout` increasing, and `executor.queued` for `@Async` pools.

#### Why does a Micrometer name differ from the name in Prometheus?

The Prometheus registry converts names to snake case, appends `_total` to counters and the base unit to timers (`_seconds`), so `orders.placed` becomes `orders_placed_total`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Expose only the endpoints needed, on a separate management port, with Spring Security and per-endpoint access settings; `env`, `heapdump` and `threaddump` disclose sensitive data.
- Liveness answers "restart me?" and must not depend on external systems; readiness answers "send traffic?"; a startup probe covers slow start-up.
- Micrometer meters are identified by name and tags; use counters, gauges and timers from a `MeterRegistry` and keep tag values bounded.
- Series count equals the product of tag cardinalities and bucket counts; never tag by identifier or raw URL.
- Publish histograms with buckets around the latency objectives; averages hide the tail and client-side percentiles cannot be aggregated.
- Organise dashboards and alerts by RED for requests and USE for resources; alert on user-visible symptoms with a `for` duration.

Logs are the record of discrete events, and during an incident they are the only source that explains why a particular request failed. Their value depends on three properties: each line can be found (consistent fields, a correlation identifier), each line is trustworthy (no forged entries, no sensitive data) and logging does not harm the service (no flooding, no blocking). Spring Boot configures logging by default; this chapter explains what is configured, how to move from text to structured JSON, how context travels in the MDC, and how to keep logging from becoming the incident.

### Concept and mechanism

#### SLF4J, Logback and what Boot sets up

Application code logs against the **SLF4J** facade (`org.slf4j.Logger`). The default backend in `spring-boot-starter-logging` is **Logback**, reached through SLF4J; bridges (`jul-to-slf4j`, `log4j-to-slf4j`, `jcl-over-slf4j`) route libraries that use other APIs into the same pipeline. A logger is named hierarchically (`shop.orders.OrderService`) and inherits the level of its nearest configured ancestor; the event then flows to the appenders of the logger and, because of additivity, of its ancestors up to the root logger.
